title: L'amour et les affaires  (Love and Business)

segments.t: At the ASK agency, tensions rise in the office corridor. Mathias and Andréa confront Gabriel about his decision to represent his girlfriend Sofia as an actress. They warn him that blending romance with professional representation spells disaster. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
Sofia a auditionné pour beaucoup de rôles.
Alors je l'aide, c'est le travail d'un agent.
Mais tu vas beaucoup trop loin.
Cette Sofia travaille à l'accueil de l'agence?
Oui, et c'est une excellente comédienne.
Tu es son agent, et tu es son amant.
Ça ne regarde personne, Mathias.
Il faut que cette situation s'arrête tout de suite.
Fais ce que tu veux, mais ne la représente pas.
Je fais ce que je veux avec mes clients.
Chaque dossier est sacré ici. Toujours.
Franchement, Gabriel, il n'a pas tort.
Ce n'est pas bon pour un couple de travailler ensemble.
Des couples légendaires travaillaient ensemble.
L'un battait sa femme, l'autre a été assassiné.
Je suis complètement à bout avec cette histoire.
Let's explore the conversation line by line and unpack the French phrases.
Sofia a auditionné pour beaucoup de rôles.
'Sofia has auditioned for many roles.' Mathias opens by describing Sofia using an action that sounds exactly like 'auditioned'. In French, it sounds perfect.
Alors je l'aide, c'est le travail d'un agent.
'So I am helping her, that is an agent's job.' Gabriel defends his supportive role using a direct cognate meaning 'agent'. This is standard in French.
Mais tu vas beaucoup trop loin.
'But you are going much too far.' Mathias cautions Gabriel using a handy phrase meaning 'too far'. A nice sentence in French.
Cette Sofia travaille à l'accueil de l'agence?
'This Sofia works at the agency reception?' Mathias asks with skepticism, pointing out her job using a cognate meaning 'reception'. A great expression in French.
Oui, et c'est une excellente comédienne.
'Yes, and she is an excellent actress.' Gabriel stands up for her talent using a term for 'actress' that literally means 'comedian'. You can say this in French.
Tu es son agent, et tu es son amant.
'You are her agent, and you are her lover.' Mathias bluntly states the dual relationship using a direct cognate meaning 'lover'. In French, this is widely used.
Ça ne regarde personne, Mathias.
'That is nobody's business, Mathias.' Gabriel pushes back using an everyday expression meaning 'that looks at nobody'. The French love this expression.
Il faut que cette situation s'arrête tout de suite.
'This situation must stop right away.' Mathias insists firmly using a strong chunk meaning 'it is necessary that'. In French, it fits perfectly.
Fais ce que tu veux, mais ne la représente pas.
'Do what you want, but do not represent her.' Mathias draws a strict line using a direct cognate meaning 'represent'. A nice way to say it in French.
Je fais ce que je veux avec mes clients.
'I do what I want with my clients.' Gabriel stubbornly defends his autonomy using a handy connector meaning 'with'. In French, it is a great choice.
Chaque dossier est sacré ici. Toujours.
'Every file is sacred here. Always.' Gabriel emphasizes his point using a cognate meaning 'sacred'. The French find this natural.
Franchement, Gabriel, il n'a pas tort.
'Frankly, Gabriel, he is not wrong.' Andréa chimes in to support Mathias using a handy expression meaning 'he has no wrong'. In French, this sounds very fluent.
Ce n'est pas bon pour un couple de travailler ensemble.
'It is not good for a couple to work together.' She warns him using an everyday term meaning 'together'. The French use this structure often.
Des couples légendaires travaillaient ensemble.
'Legendary couples worked together.' Gabriel cites historical examples using a direct cognate meaning 'legendary'. In French, this phrasing is common.
L'un battait sa femme, l'autre a été assassiné.
'One beat his wife, the other was murdered.' Andréa darkly debunks his examples using an action meaning 'was assassinated'. You will find this useful in French.
Je suis complètement à bout avec cette histoire.

'I am completely exhausted with this story.' Gabriel expresses total frustration with an idiom meaning 'at the end'. This sounds extremely natural in French. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more to lock in what you have learned.

Mathias and Andréa make their stance crystal clear: representation and romance do not mix. Gabriel finds himself caught between his personal feelings and the firm's strict professional standards. See you next time!
